claims.text: In equiaxed refractory fusion plasma-facing alloys, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are governed by competition between vacancy-mediated dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding or pinning.
A trace addition of a fast-diffusing solute can enhance the alloy's intrinsic vacancy diffusion rate.
Enhanced vacancy diffusion increases dislocation-climb activity.
Increased dislocation-climb activity reduces yield strength.
Lower yield strength together with modified or extended strain hardening can promote higher fracture toughness.
The baseline refractory alloys have equiaxed grains, pre-existing dislocation networks, and typical solute or precipitate populations.
The dopant can increase vacancy diffusion without changing grain-boundary character or precipitate distribution.
Above 1000 °C, vacancy diffusion and dislocation-climb processes are sufficiently activated in the proposed refractory alloys.
The hypothesis is restricted to conditions with negligible irradiation effects.
Vacancy-facilitated climb modulates the effectiveness of grain-boundary sliding and precipitate-induced dislocation pinning.
Accelerated dislocation climb reduces grain-boundary sliding resistance and precipitate pinning.
Changing the balance between dislocation-mediated plasticity and boundary-controlled mechanisms modifies strain hardening.
Relative to the undoped control, doped samples will exhibit lower high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the undoped control, doped samples will exhibit altered high-temperature strain-hardening behavior.
Relative to the undoped control, doped samples will exhibit higher high-temperature fracture toughness.
The proposed mechanism applies broadly to refractory and tungsten-based alloys above 1000 °C when their microstructures remain equiaxed and have conventional precipitate distributions.
Initial microstructure, temperature, strain, and strain rate influence high-temperature plastic-flow behavior.
Variations in alloy chemistry and dopant effects can change the magnitude of the yield-strength and toughness responses.
A comparison using nominally identical equiaxed microstructures, with dopant addition as the intended experimental difference, is proposed to isolate the effect of enhanced vacancy diffusion.
Absence of statistically significant reductions in yield strength, changes in strain hardening, and increases in toughness in the doped group would falsify the stated hypothesis.
